title: The wise and foolish virgins
speaker: The risen Jesus and the disciples, in dialogue
note: This discussion begins in chapter 42. It interprets the virgins differently from Matthew 25:1–13.

title: Lambs among wolves
speaker: Jesus and Peter, quoted by the author
note: The opening image resembles Matthew 10:16 and Luke 10:3. The dialogue with Peter is additional.

title: The pearl in the mud
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The dyer’s work
speaker: The author narrates; the Lord speaks
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The blind and the sighted in darkness
speaker: The author narrates; the disciples and the Savior speak
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The shepherd and the lost sheep
locator: The Parable of the Sheep · paragraphs 1–2
speaker: The author, interpreting the shepherd image
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic
note: The author interprets the lost sheep image; this is not presented here as Jesus telling the parable.

title: The jars
locator: The Parable of the Jars · paragraphs 1–2
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic
note: Selected paragraphs; the discussion continues in the edition.

title: Nightmares and waking
locator: The Parable of the Nightmares · paragraphs 1–2
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The elm and the vine
speaker: Hermas narrates; Hermas and the Shepherd speak

title: The vineyard and the servant
speaker: The Shepherd tells Hermas a parable
note: The Shepherd’s explanation continues in the edition.

title: The tower being built
speaker: Hermas narrates; the woman, who identifies herself as the Church, speaks
note: Selected paragraphs; the woman’s explanation continues in the edition.

title: Fingers, grain and trees
speaker: Jesus and the disciples, in dialogue

title: The blind leading the blind
speaker: Jesus speaks to the disciples
note: The same image appears in Matthew 15:14, Luke 6:39 and Thomas 34.

title: The vine and its fruit
speaker: The author quotes a prophetic word, then speaks

title: Two becoming one
speaker: The author quotes the Lord, then explains the saying

thomas.note: Thomas 22 includes a related saying about the two becoming one. The wording and surrounding discussion differ.

title: The householder and the food
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: Sowing in winter and reaping in summer
locator: Life, Death, Light, and Darkness · paragraph 1
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: God as a dyer
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The root of evil
speaker: The author, quoting the Word
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic
note: The axe image also appears in Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9, spoken there by John the Baptist. Philip develops the image differently.

title: The fruit of knowledge
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The unopened will
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The children as fragrance
speaker: The author
translator: Mark M. Mattison · translation from the Coptic

title: The two cities
locator: Parables Which He Spake With Me · paragraphs 1–11
speaker: The Shepherd speaks to Hermas

title: Trees in winter and summer
speaker: Hermas and the Shepherd speak
note: Two adjacent similitudes compare trees in winter and summer.

title: The two shepherds
speaker: Hermas narrates; Hermas and the Shepherd speak

title: The willow and its branches
speaker: Hermas narrates; the Shepherd and the angel Michael speak

title: The tower and the twelve mountains
speaker: Hermas narrates; the Shepherd, the virgins and the six men speak
note: This vision revisits and expands the tower shown in Vision 3.

title: The two ways of life and death
speaker: The author’s instruction
note: Compare Barnabas 18–20: the writings use related two-ways instruction with different wording.

title: The ways of light and darkness
speaker: The author’s instruction
note: A related form of the two-ways instruction appears in the Didache.

title: The scattered bread gathered together
speaker: A prayer of thanksgiving
note: The prayer compares the gathered bread with the gathering of the church.

title: The vine and its seasons
speaker: An unidentified scripture quoted by the author
note: A related quotation appears in 2 Clement 11; its original source is uncertain.

title: The seed and the harvest
speaker: The author
note: The author uses the sowing and growth of seed as an image of resurrection.

title: Soldiers and members of the body
speaker: The author
note: The image of the body and its members can also be compared with 1 Corinthians 12:12–27.

title: The soul and the body
speaker: The author
note: The author compares Christians in the world to the soul in the body.

title: A report of three servants
speaker: Eusebius summarizing a gospel written in Hebrew letters
note: Eusebius summarizes the story and comments on Matthew; the identity of the gospel is debated. Epanalepsis means returning to a prior subject. James’s explanatory parenthesis is omitted.

title: The Hymn of the Pearl
speaker: Thomas recites the hymn; a prince narrates and others speak within it
note: The hymn appears in some manuscripts of the Acts. Its origin and interpretation are debated. Angle and square brackets mark the translator’s supplements; daggers mark uncertain text. His variant notes are omitted. Line breaks are reading aids.

title: Lamps and sheep turned to wolves
speaker: The author
note: The lamps and readiness resemble Luke 12:35–40 and Matthew 25:1–13, but this passage tells no story of bridesmaids. Here sheep turn into wolves, unlike the sheep sent among wolves in Matthew 10:16 and Luke 10:3.

title: Animals and the food laws
speaker: The author
translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson · translation
note: The author interprets the food laws through animal images. Several claims about animal behavior and reproduction are false.

title: The tree beside water
speaker: The author
note: The author quotes and interprets a tree by water; Matthew and Luke use trees and fruit in a different comparison.

title: The spiritual temple
speaker: The author
note: The author explains the temple as a dwelling within people.

title: The phoenix
speaker: The author
note: The author presents the traditional phoenix legend as an image of resurrection. It is not a biological account.

title: The gate of righteousness
speaker: The author
note: The author quotes Psalm 118:19–20. John 10:7–9 uses a door image in a different setting.

title: A king sending his son
speaker: The author
note: The author compares the sending of the Son to a king sending his son.

title: The garden and its trees
speaker: The author
note: The closing section uses the garden and its trees as images.

title: The hymn of the bride
speaker: Thomas sings
note: The wedding and banquet imagery is a partial comparison: Thomas’s song does not retell the Gospel parables. Angle brackets and daggers mark the translator’s editorial text.

title: The palace built for the king
speaker: The narrator; Thomas, King Gundaphorus, Gad and others speak
note: This is an episode in the Acts, not a parable spoken by Jesus. The heavenly palace can be compared thematically with Matthew 6:19–21 and Luke 12:33–34. Parentheses include the translator’s notes.

title: Thomas’s prayer and its images
speaker: Thomas prays
note: James follows an alternative manuscript form; he notes that manuscript U omits nearly all of section 147. Thomas prays using wheat and weeds, a vine, money, a supper, a wedding, a lamp, a plough and a harvest. The plough recalls Luke 9:62. The Gospel passages use these images in different settings; the prayer is not a retelling of any one parable. Parentheses include James’s textual notes.

title: The vine of David
speaker: A thanksgiving prayer
note: The vine is a shared image with John 15; the prayers and setting differ.

title: What is holy and the dogs
speaker: The author quotes the Lord
note: The words about dogs resemble Matthew 7:6; this passage does not include the pearls and pigs.

title: The teacher and the worker
speaker: The author
note: The support of teachers is compared with a worker’s support; the Gospel passages concern those sent out.

title: The measure used
speaker: The author quotes the Lord Jesus
note: The sayings resemble Matthew 7:2, Mark 4:24, and Luke 6:38; their wording and settings differ.

title: The body and the millstone
speaker: The author and the author quoting Jesus
translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson · translation
note: The millstone saying resembles Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42, and Luke 17:2; the wording differs.

title: The race and the contest
speaker: The author
note: 1 Clement uses the race for examples of endurance; 2 Clement’s contest develops a different comparison.

title: The harmony of creation
speaker: The author
translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson · translation
note: The author describes nature as an example of peace and harmony.

title: The fountain and the nest
speaker: The author quotes the prophets
note: The fountain recalls living water in John 4:13–14, but these quotations have a different setting.

title: Moses and the bronze serpent
speaker: The author interprets Scripture
note: Barnabas interprets Moses’s raised arms and the serpent as signs. John 3:14–15 also refers to the serpent, in a different passage.

title: The ransom and the exchange
speaker: The author
note: The writer uses ransom, covering and exchange imagery.

title: The bride chamber and the marriage
speaker: The narrator and Jesus in the narrative
note: This noncanonical narrative attributes the speech to Jesus and presents an ascetic view of marriage; the bridegroom imagery differs from the Gospel scene.

title: The bride’s response
speaker: The bride
note: The bride speaks of marriage and her new hope. The bridegroom image differs from the Gospel scene.

title: The shepherd and the flock
speaker: Thomas prays; the narrator, king and Gad speak
note: This prayer follows the palace story. Shepherd, sheep and wolves are shared images; the settings differ.

title: The crowd and the high places
speaker: Thomas speaks; the narrator sets the scene
note: Thomas makes an analogy from the crowd climbing to see him, then calls Jesus a physician. The Gospel physician saying uses the image in a different setting.

title: The bitter tree and its fruit
speaker: Thomas speaks
note: The tree and fruit resemble the Gospel images, but Thomas applies them differently.

title: The burden and the yoke
speaker: The narrator and Thomas; Thomas quotes the Lord
note: Thomas quotes an invitation to the burdened and later calls meekness a yoke. James follows a corrupt manuscript U; P is shorter and omits section 85, and the Syriac differs.

title: The seed of the words
speaker: Thomas and Mygdonia speak
note: Receiving seed and bearing fruit recalls the sower’s explanation in Mark 4:14–20; this is not a retelling of the whole parable.

title: Mygdonia on the bridegroom
speaker: Charisius and Mygdonia speak
note: The bridegroom image is shared with the Gospel passages, but Mygdonia speaks in an ascetic discussion of marriage. James marks uncertain and variant wording.

title: The king and the soldiers
speaker: Thomas and King Misdaeus speak
note: Thomas compares service to a king with service to God. The clothing differs from the wedding guest’s garment.

title: The tower, spring and treasure
speaker: Thomas, Mygdonia and Charisius speak
note: Mygdonia asks why someone would tear down a tower or fill in a spring. Luke’s builder considers whether he can finish a tower. James marks the tower-building words as supplied; the treasure image also differs from Matthew 13:44.

title: The fruit and the oil
speaker: The narrator; Thomas prays
note: Thomas addresses the oil with fruit and tree imagery. James marks uncertain and variant wording.

title: The physician of souls
speaker: Thomas prays
note: Thomas addresses Jesus as a physician of souls. The Gospel saying uses the physician image in a different setting.

title: The birds and the light burden
speaker: Thomas speaks and quotes the Saviour
note: Thomas recalls the sayings about birds and tomorrow, then the light burden. His wording and setting differ from the Gospel accounts.

title: Wealth, clothing and lasting gifts
speaker: Thomas speaks
note: Thomas quotes sayings about wealth and fine clothing, and recalls the instruction not to worry about food and clothing. The comparisons show related sayings in different settings. James notes Syriac variants in this passage.

title: Ask, seek and knock
speaker: Thomas prays and quotes Jesus
note: Thomas recalls the saying in a prayer. The Gospel accounts present the saying in their own teaching settings.

title: The physician of souls and Mygdonia
speaker: Mygdonia and Charisius speak
note: Mygdonia describes Thomas as a physician of souls; the Gospel saying uses the physician image for Jesus in a different setting.

title: The physician of all
speaker: The narrator and Thomas
note: Thomas speaks of Jesus as a physician. James marks supplied words with angle brackets and notes Syriac variants; the Gospel saying has a different setting.

title: The physician and the flock
speaker: Thomas prays
note: Thomas addresses Jesus as a physician and a shepherd. The Gospel physician saying uses a shared image in a different setting. James notes Greek and Syriac variants.

title: The diligent and careless workers
speaker: The author
note: The author contrasts workers. The talents, pounds and servant sayings have different settings and are not retold here.

title: The mirror and the light
speaker: The author
note: The author uses images of a mirror, sight and light.

title: The stone the builders rejected
speaker: The author interprets Scripture
translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson · translation
note: The author quotes the rejected stone from Psalm 118. The Gospel accounts and Thomas 66 also quote it; Barnabas does not retell the tenants story. This selection contains the full chapter.

title: The milk and honey
speaker: The author
note: The author interprets the promised land and compares nourishment with faith and the word. The feeding description is part of the ancient text.

title: The goats and the thorns
speaker: The author
note: The author interprets goats and wool among thorns as figures of Jesus and affliction. This is the author’s interpretation.

title: The neighbor’s burden
speaker: The author
note: The author uses the image of carrying a neighbor’s burden while describing acts of help.

title: The king’s wedding invitation
speaker: The narrator, townspeople, Abbanes and Thomas
note: The king’s summons is an event in this narrative, not a parable. It shares a royal wedding invitation with Matthew; Luke’s banquet has a different setting.

title: Putting on the new person in prayer
speaker: Thomas prays to Jesus
note: Thomas prays that the hearers put off the old person and put on the new. Compare Ephesians 4:22–24 and Colossians 3:9–10; this is not a Jesus parable.

title: The woman called a straying sheep
speaker: A woman recounts words spoken in her vision
note: The woman recounts being called a straying sheep. The Gospel stories describe a shepherd searching; this account does not.

title: Putting off the old person
speaker: Thomas addresses the crowd
note: Thomas uses the clothing image as an instruction. Compare Ephesians 4:22–24 and Colossians 3:9–10; this is not a Jesus parable.

title: The burden and heat of the day
speaker: Thomas prays to Jesus
note: Thomas prays for those who bear the day’s burden and heat. Matthew’s vineyard workers use similar words in a different story.

title: The flock and the wolves
speaker: Thomas prays for the community
note: Thomas asks for protection for Xenophon’s flock. The Gospels use sheep and wolves in different settings.

title: Wolves in sheep’s clothing
speaker: A wild ass speaks to the crowd
note: The speaker warns about false apostles and prophets. Matthew 7:15 uses the same image for false prophets; the speakers and settings differ.

title: Thoughts taken away
speaker: Thomas speaks to believers
note: Thomas warns that Satan might take their thoughts. The sower’s explanation concerns the word being taken away; the comparison is partial.

title: Many called, few chosen
speaker: The author quotes a saying
note: The words resemble Matthew 22:14. The author does not retell the wedding banquet, and the source of the quotation is not identified here.

title: The net spread for birds
speaker: The author quotes and interprets Scripture
note: The author interprets a saying about a net spread for birds. Matthew’s parable uses a fishing net in a different comparison.

title: The shepherd struck and the sheep scattered
speaker: The author quotes a prophetic saying
note: The author and the Gospel accounts quote the shepherd saying from Zechariah 13:7. Their wording and settings differ.

title: The red heifer
speaker: The author interprets a ritual
note: The author gives a symbolic interpretation of the heifer and its purification rite. This is an interpretation, not a parable told by Jesus.

title: Thorns and the heart
speaker: The author quotes and interprets Scripture
note: The quotation includes sowing among thorns. The sower parable uses a similar image in a different setting.

title: Scarlet and snow
speaker: The author quotes prophetic words
note: The author quotes words about repentance, including Isaiah’s image of scarlet sins becoming white as snow.

title: Rahab’s scarlet thread
speaker: The author recounts and interprets the spies’ words
note: The author gives a symbolic interpretation of the scarlet thread in Rahab’s story.

title: Gathered from the four winds
speaker: A prayer of thanksgiving
note: The prayer asks for the church to be gathered. Matthew and Mark describe a gathering from the four winds in a different setting.

title: Sojourners and citizens
speaker: The author describes Christians
note: The author describes Christians as sojourners and speaks of citizenship in heaven. The next chapter compares Christians to the soul in the body.
